amendments.rule: Rule 22's head-on-the-nominal-word is scoped to a substantival **article**, and a relative **pronoun** expanded by a supplied word is decided by which of the two words carries content. Where the supplied word is a bare antecedent or determiner, the relativizer is the head, because the pronoun's own lexeme is what *which* or *whom* spells: `ἣν εἴχομεν ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς` → *that which we had from the beginning* heads on *which*, as *he whom*, *him whom*, *him of whom* and *of that which* do, fifteen units against three. Where the supplied word is a **generic noun**, it is the nominal the relative substantivizes and it takes the head: `ἃ εἰργασάμεθα` → *the things which we have wrought* heads on *things*, as JHN.8.26, JHN.8.38, JHN.11.46, JHN.12.50, JHN.15.14 and TIT.2.1 read *the things which* and GAL.1.20 reads *touching the things which* — fifteen units against four, of which REV.2.10 and REV.4.1 give no head reasoning at all, JHN.18.21 asserts rule 17 without argument, and TIT.1.11 is `medium` conceding the nominal. The substantival article is the contrast and it is unanimous the other way: `τὸ` → *that which* heads on *that* in all nine corpus units and on the relativizer in none, and every article expanded with *things* heads on *things*, because an article's own lexeme is a determiner and the relativizer is supplied for it. So the test is whether the supplied word has content of its own — *things* names what is referred to, *that* only points at it — which is rule 17's principle rather than an exception to it. Rule 17's generic-noun clause is not the contrast, being scoped to a substantival adjective or demonstrative whose own English word already carries the sense, as `ταῦτα` → *these things* and `Πολλά` → *many things* do; there the supplied noun is the empty completion, and here the relativizer is. That such a supplied word rides **inside the relative pronoun's own unit** is presupposed by every reading above and is not left open: an antecedent the Greek does not express is a rule 7 helper on the relative that licenses it, so do not mark it `added` under rule 5, and do not hand it to a neighbouring token whose own English the ASV has already written. `Οὗτος ἦν ὃν εἶπον` → *This was he of whom I said* gives *This* to the demonstrative, a bare *was* to the copula and *he of whom* to the relative headed on *whom*, as `ὑπὲρ οὗ ἐγὼ εἶπον` → *of whom I said* gives the discontinuous *he … whom* to the relative and *of* to the expressed preposition under rules 15 and 36, and as `Ὃν ἔγραψεν Μωϋσῆς` → *him of whom Moses … wrote* does. An **indefinite** antecedent is no different and is not evidence of anything else: `ὃν ὑμεῖς οὐκ οἴδατε` → *one whom ye know not* gives *one whom* to the relative. Rule 103 is the contrast and is narrow: its `added` reaches a **repeated** antecedent, a lexical noun the verse has already spent, as 2CO.3.7 has it in terms, and it does not reach a bare pronoun or indefinite the ASV supplies where the Greek expressed none, the relative standing there unspent to license it. Rule 11 does not decide this either way, the ASV italicizing such an antecedent only sometimes.
amendments.why: JHN.1 analysed one construction four ways — folded into the relative at 1:45, given to the copula at 1:15, given to the demonstrative at 1:30, and marked `added` at 1:26 — because rule 77 fixed the head of such a unit without ever saying that the supplied antecedent belongs to that unit at all. The added clause makes explicit what rule 77's own fifteen corpus units (*he whom*, *him whom*, *him of whom*) already do, names rule 103's repeated-antecedent contrast so that it cannot be read as overturning 2CO.3.7, and records the discontinuous case where an expressed preposition stands between the antecedent and the relativizer. Everything rule 77 already said is preserved verbatim.

amendments.rule: Where a **substantival** article stands before a participle and the ASV writes only **one** English word for the pair, that word is the pronoun rule 32 gives the article, and the participle keeps its own verb and any supplied copula. `οἱ ἐπηρεάζοντες` → *who revile* gives *who* to the article and *revile* to the participle, as EPH.1.19, EPH.2.11, EPH.2.14, GAL.1.4, JHN.6.33, REV.1.4, REV.1.8, REV.2.18, REV.2.20, REV.4.8, REV.7.10, REV.8.13, REV.11.17, REV.12.10, REV.15.7, REV.16.5 and REV.16.9 do — about twenty-eight units, of which only EPH.2.11 and EPH.2.14 are hedged and neither concedes the other reading. A single relativizer is pronoun and relativizer at once, so rule 32's *and nothing else* limits what the article may absorb beyond the pronoun rather than denying it one: `οἱ κατοικοῦντες` → *they that dwell* still splits, and where the ASV writes two words the ordinary split applies, as *He* / *that would* and *every man* / *that asketh* do. Rule 31 is the contrast and its test is unchanged: where the article governs an expressed head noun the relativizer is the participle's helper and the article is `unrepresented`, and this rule blesses no unit in which a head noun is expressed. JHN.1.18 stood in the enumeration above and no longer does: its `ὁ ὢν εἰς τὸν κόλπον τοῦ πατρός` follows the expressed head noun `υἱός`, so it falls on rule 31's side, and its chapter reconciliation reread it there with the article `unrepresented` and *who is* the participle's. Count the head noun before counting the English words, and do not read a citation list as a licence where the rule's own scope excludes the unit. Rule 80 is untouched, another source word having already taken the one English word there, and so is rule 22, which speaks of no participle following. EPH.4.10 alone reads it the other way and is `medium`, which is rule 71's shape rather than rule 67's genuinely divided case. A reference comparison will report such an article as represented, and that is not a correction.
amendments.why: Rule 90's enumeration cited JHN.1.18 as precedent for aligning the article to the relativizer, but that unit has an expressed head noun — huios, on the reading the projection selects — and so falls outside the scope rule 90 itself states two sentences later. JHN.1's reconciliation reread it under rule 31 along with 1:29 and 1:40; leaving the citation in place would leave a binding rule pointing at a unit that now reads the other way, and would keep teaching the miscount. Only the citation, the count and one explanatory sentence change; every substantive clause of rule 90 is preserved verbatim.

conventions: Where the ASV renders both emprosthen mou and protos mou as *before me* in the same clause pair (1:15, 1:30), align each collocation separately and do not read either as a second realization of the other; the ASV's own gloss (Greek first in regard of me) is what fixes protos as the temporal-priority word.

ek rendered by the two-word *out of* (1:32, 1:46) is one aligned unit headed on *out*: the *of* belongs to the preposition's own English expression and is not a case marker to be split onto the governed noun.

report: Read all 60 candidate groups and the dump end to end. Most differences are ASV renderings the source licenses: hina as *that* and as bare *to* (rule 40 names this), ek as *of*/*from*/*out of*, hoti recitative-empty at 1:20 and 1:32 against causal *for* at 1:16, 1:17 and *Because* at 1:50 (rule 43), para empty at 1:40 only because the ASV realizes it nowhere there (rule 36). Those are not splits.

Split 1: the supplied English antecedent of a relative pronoun, analysed four ways. 1:45 folds it into the relative (hon -> *him of whom*, headed on *whom*); 1:15 gave *he* to the copula; 1:30 gave *he* to the demonstrative; 1:26 marked *one* `added`, though the ASV does not italicize it there. Nothing in the source licenses the difference. Rule 77's own corpus (fifteen units of *he whom*, *him whom*, *him of whom*) settles it. 1:15, 1:26 and 1:30 corrected to match 1:45.

Split 2: a second attributive article standing after an expressed head and governing a participle. 1:18, 1:29 and 1:40 aligned it to the English relativizer, while 1:9's parallel article is unrepresented. Rule 31 decides it the other way (to theo to ktisanti -> *God who created* empties the article and gives *who* to the participle), and rule 90 says in terms that it blesses no unit in which a head noun is expressed. All three corrected; at 1:40 rule 32's apposition clause reaches the same answer, ton duo having already written the antecedent.

Rule 21 breach found while rewriting those two verses: tou patros (1:18) and tou kosmou (1:29) gave *of* to the noun and a bare *the* to the article. Rule 21's tou pleromatos -> *of the fulness* makes *of the* one unit headed on *the*, the noun standing alone; corrected in both. The chapter's other genitives are already right, tou theou staying empty because the ASV writes it no determiner.

BSB disagreements adjudicated. 1:11 ta is a genuine error: rules 47 and 54 cite ta idia -> *his own* verbatim, giving *his* to the article and *own* to the adjective because idios cannot say whose; corrected, and the same verse's hoi idioi retuned to rule 31's predicate-adjective split (*they that* / *were his own*). 1:19 tou (article before a name, rule 23) and 1:41 ton (the possessive carried by idios, rule 47 citing ton adelphon ton idion verbatim) are documented convention differences, not errors.
The patches create three new BSB disagreements, at 1:18, 1:29 and 1:40; rules 31 and 32 say such reports are not corrections. No edge was changed to move an aggregate.

Left standing: 1:18's added *him* (supplied object of exegesato). Rule 103's resumptive-pronoun contrast would instead fold it onto theon under rule 15; single instance, no cross-verse dimension, kept as accepted with the alternative recorded in its note.
